whyChoose.title: What California Law Means for Your Claim

items.title: You Have Time, But Not Forever
items.desc: California generally gives you two years from the date of injury to file a claim. Claims against a government entity can require notice in as little as six months, so it's worth checking sooner rather than later.

items.title: Being Partly at Fault Doesn't End Your Claim
items.desc: California follows pure comparative fault, meaning you can still recover compensation even if you were partially responsible for the accident. Your recovery is simply reduced by your share of fault.

items.title: No Cap on Pain and Suffering
items.desc: In ordinary injury cases, California does not limit the amount you can seek for non-economic damages like pain and suffering. This is different from some states that impose strict caps.

items.title: No Upfront Cost to Get Help
items.desc: We work on contingency, meaning we only get paid if you recover compensation. This lets you get legal help without worrying about hourly fees or retainers.

items.question: How long do I have to file a personal injury claim in Buellton?
items.answer: In most cases, California law gives you two years from the date of the injury to file a claim. If a government entity was involved, such as a city vehicle or road defect, the notice period can be as short as six months. It's best to look into your situation as early as possible to avoid missing a deadline.

items.question: Where do crashes tend to happen in Buellton?
items.answer: Based on public crash records, reported collisions in Buellton show higher counts along Rt 246, Avenue Of Flags, Avenue Of The Flags, and 2nd Street, with activity often clustering on Thursday afternoons between 4 and 6 p.m. These are simply the corridors with the most recorded incidents, not a judgment about any particular road.

items.question: What if I was partly responsible for the accident?
items.answer: California uses a pure comparative fault system, so being partially at fault doesn't prevent you from recovering compensation. Your total recovery is adjusted to reflect your share of responsibility, but you're not automatically barred from a claim.

items.question: Is there a limit on what I can recover for pain and suffering?
items.answer: In typical personal injury cases, California does not cap non-economic damages such as pain and suffering. The specific amount depends on the facts of your case, which is something we can evaluate.
